 Rainy season arrives abruptly; but will the soaking continue? 
 First significant snow of the season on tap in higher Cascades 
 By Mark Nelsen Published : Oct. 26, 2026 at 9:39 PM PDT | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google Well that accelerated quickly! Did you get the impression just 5 days ago that we would stay dry this week? That was the plan...but it didn’t work out.
 The early/mid part of last week I was harping on the idea that “there’s no obvious start to the rainy season” through the end of October (this week). Some forecast models were pushing one weak system, an upper-level low” near the region briefly Sunday, then backing it offshore. Sure, maybe some showers Sunday, but then this work week would be dry. 
 Nope! 
 Instead, with just 2-3 days notice, all forecast models decided that upper-level low would just linger around the region all this week! That includes several reinforcing shots of cool air coming down out of Canada later in the week. It’s actually somewhat rare (nowadays) that a significant change in the general upper-level pattern goes undetected so close to the change itself. In this case it brought the first soaking rains in many weeks. But will this lead to a long wet period? Yes and No.
 I believe it IS the beginning of the rainy season, but there will probably be a break in the rain for a few days early next week.
 You can see the weak trough overhead now, several embedded waves of showers rotating through the trough
 Right now (kptv) Then a colder dip in the jet stream (trough) arrives Friday. This would bring snow down to 1,000-2,000′ in winter, but only down to around 3,000′ this early in the cool season.
 Friday Evening (kptv) That low was forecast to stay well offshore at one point...but...bygones...
 This tells me showers will be lingering Friday and Saturday, although it’s important to point out this isn’t a stormy pattern at all. Notice we have no strong westerly jet in place for strong wind or flooding rains. By early next week, some sort of ridging takes over for awhile. This should give us at least 2-4 days of dry weather starting Sunday the 1st.
 Monday the 2nd (kptv) I noticed the ECMWF ensemble 24-hour rainfall shows a nice gap during this time; I’m aiming for at least a couple of bike rides during that time. Notice we seem to be heading toward a wet pattern again soon after that time (around the 5th or so).
 (kptv) That’s because there are hints that a typical El Niño pattern may set up after that time along the West Coast. Much stormier in the Eastern Pacific, but more energy headed south of us and/or staying offshore as high pressure develops over southern Canada. This is the 500mb 10-15 day anomaly showing that very different pattern vs. what we have right now. This is a mild to warm November weather pattern and can be quite wet.
 November 5th-10th (kptv) SUMMARY
 Expect cool showers to linger through Halloween, exact timing and intensity impossible to track. 
 Showers become lighter Thursday through Halloween, less than 1″ more likely in western valleys this week 
 Next dry spell? Early next week 
 The wet season is here, with just occasional, brief dry periods on tap now through at least March. A major soaking is possible at some point after the 5th of November. 
 Temperatures? We’re done with 80s and 70s for this year. Get used to 50s and lower 60s for afternoon highs 
 CASCADE SNOW
 The cool systems this week will drop lots of snow at/above 6,000′ in the Cascades, but very little at pass elevations. Our GRAF model snow forecast shows that nicely. Snow levels should bottom out around 3,000′ Thursday and Friday mornings.
 (kptv) After a dry period early next week, warmer systems will likely bring more rain than snow to the Cascades. So the 1-2′ snow that falls in the high Cascades this week will likely melt. I know, I’m holding a ski pass right now, ready to go. But I don’t think it’s happening in the next 10 days. If you are driving through the Cascades, Thursday through Saturday mornings could feature a bit of snow on the passes, but it’ll be patchy. Plan to travel midday and afternoons if you hate seeing snow.
 (kptv) If you are reading this, you probably have a strong interest in weather. We’ve got two additional ways to get detailed weather information. It’s not A.I. slop and not automated, we spend a lot of time on these and enjoy producing them. Check them out! 
 FIRST ALERT WEATHER EXTRA SHOW (FAWX) 
 Did you know we are producing a DAILY (most weekdays) weather show at KPTV? I’m not aware of any other station in our area doing this. It’s typically 30 minutes of detailed weather information from our meteorologists. We take a deep dive into explainers and data that we don’t have time for on regular broadcast TV. Basically we have all the time in the world to talk about weather! Find old episodes here on our web page:
 www.kptv.com/video-gallery/weather/first-alert-weather-extras/ 
 These are LIVE at 7 p.m. on our FOX 12 OREGON streaming app. You add that on your Roku, Amazon Fire, or SmartTV. I know, seems complicated, but it’s just another little app right beside your Netflix, Amazon, HBO, etc... apps. That’s how mine is set up at home. These are on the web page typically by 8 p.m. or so if you can’t watch live.
 FIRST ALERT WEATHER PODCAST 
 It’s still going strong! We record an episode most Wednesdays or Thursdays at 7 p.m., full of detailed weather information and a few laughs. We typically stream it live at the same time on our FOX 12 WEATHER Facebook page so that you can ask questions too. Within about 1.5 hours it’s on our web page (and app) here:
 www.kptv.com/podcasts/weather/ 
 We also play the podcast on our FAWX show too.
